value.overview: The Black-throated Wren (Pheugopedius atrogularis) is a small, secretive songbird of humid forests in Central America. It belongs to the wren family and is usually detected by its loud, repeated song rather than by prolonged views. The species forages in dense vegetation close to the ground, often in pairs or family groups. Its range extends from southeastern Nicaragua through Costa Rica to western Panama, with Costa Rica forming an important part of its distribution.
value.classification: The Black-throated Wren is a member of the wren family, Troglodytidae, and the genus Pheugopedius. It is generally treated as a distinct species and was formerly grouped with the Sooty-headed Wren.
value.identification: This is a compact, medium-sized wren with warm brown to rufous-brown upperparts, a strongly contrasting dark throat and upper breast, and paler lower underparts. The wings and tail show darker barring, while the face has contrasting pale and dark markings. It is often difficult to see because it moves through tangled undergrowth, fallen leaves, vines, and low shrubs. Its distinctive, forceful song is frequently the most reliable way to locate it.
value.rangeHabitat: The Black-throated Wren occurs from southeastern Nicaragua through eastern and Caribbean Costa Rica to western Panama. In Costa Rica it is primarily associated with humid Caribbean-slope lowlands and foothills, including mature forest, forest edges, dense second growth, and plantations or gardens with thick understory. It is regularly recorded in areas such as the northern lowlands, the Sarapiquí region, Arenal, and the Caribbean foothills. It generally favors shaded, structurally complex vegetation rather than open habitats.
value.migrationStatus: Resident in Costa Rica and throughout its range; it is not considered a long-distance migrant. Individuals may make short local movements in response to food availability or habitat conditions.
value.breeding: The species is thought to breed during the wet-season or early wet-season periods typical of much of its Central American range, although timing varies geographically. Like related Pheugopedius wrens, it uses dense vegetation and sheltered sites near the ground for nesting. Reported nests are enclosed or partly enclosed structures made from plant fibers and other debris. Pairs defend territories with coordinated songs, and both adults may participate in nest building, incubation, and care of the young.
value.dietFeeding: The Black-throated Wren feeds mainly on insects and other small invertebrates found among leaf litter, vines, moss, bark, and low vegetation. It searches methodically through dense cover, hopping between stems and probing leaves or debris. Small spiders and other arthropods are likely important food items. Its low, concealed feeding style makes it more often heard than seen, especially in humid forest understory.
value.behavior: This wren is active, vocal, and highly territorial. It commonly travels in pairs or small family groups and keeps close to dense cover while moving through the understory. The species frequently responds to recordings or nearby birds with vigorous calling and song. It may remain hidden while giving repeated phrases from tangled vegetation. Cooperative or duet-like vocal behavior is characteristic of many related wrens and may help maintain pair bonds and territory boundaries.

conservation.populationTrend: The global population trend is not precisely quantified, but the species is not currently considered to meet the criteria for a threatened category.
